difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: one concept (insertion-sort swaps equal the number of inversions) applied in 2-3 routine steps to four candidate values, with a trap in forgetting the inversion (15, 13) already present; about 1.5-2 min for a prepared student.
stem: Suppose that insertion sort is applied to the array $[1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, x, 15, 13]$ and it takes exactly two swaps to sort the array. Select all possible values of $x$.

solution.quick: Insertion sort performs one swap per **inversion** (a pair $i < j$ with $a_i > a_j$). Without $x$ the array already has exactly one inversion, $(15, 13)$, so $x$ must be part of exactly one more. $x = 10$ (only $11 > 10$ before it) and $x = 14$ (only $13 < 14$ after it) qualify; $x = 12$ gives $1$ swap and $x = 16$ gives $3$. Answer **(A), (C)**.

steps.title: Swaps in insertion sort = number of inversions
steps.body:
Insertion sort takes each element $a_i$ in turn and moves it left, swapping it with its left neighbour while that neighbour is larger:

```text
for i = 1 .. n-1:
    j = i
    while j > 0 and a[j-1] > a[j]:
        swap a[j-1], a[j]
        j = j - 1
```

An **inversion** is a pair of positions $i < j$ with $a_i > a_j$. Each swap exchanges two *adjacent* elements that are out of order, so it removes exactly one inversion and creates none. The sort stops when no inversions remain, hence

$$
\text{number of swaps} = \text{number of inversions in the input.}
$$

steps.title: Inversions that do not involve $x$
steps.body:
Ignore $x$ and look at the other eight values in order: $1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 15, 13$.

- $1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11$ are increasing, so no inversions among them.
- Every one of them is smaller than both $15$ and $13$, so no inversions between the prefix and $\{15, 13\}$.
- $15$ comes before $13$: **one** inversion, $(15, 13)$.

So the array already needs $1$ swap without $x$. For exactly two swaps, $x$ must take part in **exactly one** inversion.

steps.title: Inversions involving $x$ for each option
steps.body:
$x$ sits at position 7. Its inversions are the elements **before** it that are larger than $x$ (from $1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11$) plus the elements **after** it that are smaller than $x$ (from $15, 13$).

| $x$ | Before $x$ and $> x$ | After $x$ and $< x$ | Inversions with $x$ | Total swaps $= 1 + \text{(previous column)}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $10$ | $11$ | none | $1$ | $2$ |
| $12$ | none | none | $0$ | $1$ |
| $14$ | none | $13$ | $1$ | $2$ |
| $16$ | none | $15, 13$ | $2$ | $3$ |

Exactly two swaps occur for $x = 10$ and $x = 14$.

steps.title: Confirm by tracing the sort
steps.body:
Positions $1$ to $6$ are already sorted, so the first swap can happen only when position $7$ is inserted.

- **$x = 10$:** insert $10$: $10 < 11$, swap $\Rightarrow [1,3,5,7,9,10,11,15,13]$; then $9 < 10$, stop. Insert $15$: $11 < 15$, no swap. Insert $13$: $13 < 15$, swap $\Rightarrow [\ldots,11,13,15]$; then $11 < 13$, stop. **2 swaps.**
- **$x = 12$:** $12$ and $15$ are already in place; inserting $13$ needs one swap past $15$. **1 swap.**
- **$x = 14$:** $14$ and $15$ are in place. Insert $13$: swap past $15$ $\Rightarrow [\ldots,11,14,13,15]$, swap past $14$ $\Rightarrow [\ldots,11,13,14,15]$; then $11 < 13$, stop. **2 swaps.**
- **$x = 16$:** insert $15$: $15 < 16$, swap $\Rightarrow [\ldots,11,15,16,13]$. Insert $13$: swap past $16$, swap past $15$ $\Rightarrow [\ldots,11,13,15,16]$. **3 swaps.**

The traces agree with the inversion count: the possible values are $10$ and $14$, options **(A)** and **(C)**.

solution.teaching:
**How insertion sort works.** Insertion sort grows a sorted prefix one element at a time. At step $i$, the prefix $a_1, \ldots, a_{i-1}$ is already sorted, and the new element $a_i$ is moved left past every larger element in the prefix until it meets one that is not larger. In the swap-based version each move is one swap of adjacent elements; in the shift-based version each move is one shift. The count is the same either way.

**Inversions measure how unsorted an array is.** An inversion is a pair of positions $i < j$ whose values are out of order ($a_i > a_j$). A sorted array has $0$ inversions, and a reverse-sorted array of $n$ distinct values has the maximum $\binom{n}{2} = n(n-1)/2$.

**Why swaps equal inversions.** Swapping two adjacent out-of-order elements changes the relative order of only that one pair, so it removes exactly one inversion and cannot create any. Insertion sort only ever swaps adjacent out-of-order pairs and finishes with zero inversions, so the total number of swaps is exactly the number of inversions in the input. This is also why insertion sort runs in $\Theta(n + I)$ time, where $I$ is the inversion count: it is fast ($\Theta(n)$) on nearly sorted inputs and $\Theta(n^2)$ on reverse-sorted ones.

**Counting inversions for one element.** The inversions that involve a particular element $v$ are: the elements *before* $v$ that are larger than $v$, plus the elements *after* $v$ that are smaller than $v$.

**Back to the question.** Apart from $x$, the array $[1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, \_, 15, 13]$ has one inversion, $(15, 13)$. Two swaps in total therefore means $x$ must be out of order with exactly one other element. With distinct values, that happens when $x$ lies just below $11$ (between $9$ and $11$, e.g. $10$) or just above $13$ (between $13$ and $15$, e.g. $14$). $x = 12$ fits between $11$ and $13$ with no inversion (1 swap in total), and $x = 16$ is larger than both $15$ and $13$ (3 swaps in total). So the answer is (A) and (C).

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: $x = 10$: one inversion with $x$ (the $11$ before it) plus the existing $(15, 13)$ gives $2$ swaps.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: $x = 12$ is already in its correct place ($11 < 12 < 13$), so it adds no inversion. Only $(15, 13)$ remains: $1$ swap, not $2$.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: $x = 14$: one inversion with $x$ (the $13$ after it) plus the existing $(15, 13)$ gives $2$ swaps. The $13$ is swapped past $15$ and then past $14$.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: $x = 16$ is larger than both $15$ and $13$ that follow it, giving $2$ inversions with $x$ plus $(15, 13)$: $3$ swaps, not $2$.

solution.shortcut: Swaps = inversions. The array already has one inversion, $(15, 13)$, so $x$ must be out of order with exactly **one** element: count (larger elements before $x$) + (smaller elements after $x$) and keep the options where this equals $1$.
solution.commonTrap: Forgetting that $(15, 13)$ is already an inversion and looking for an $x$ that creates two inversions by itself; that wrongly picks $x = 16$ (D), which actually needs $3$ swaps. Another slip is counting comparisons instead of swaps.

answerVerification.checkCode:
def insertion_sort_swaps(a):
    a, swaps = list(a), 0
    for i in range(1, len(a)):
        j = i
        while j > 0 and a[j - 1] > a[j]:          # swap-based insertion sort
            a[j - 1], a[j] = a[j], a[j - 1]; swaps += 1; j -= 1
    assert a == sorted(a)
    return swaps
inv = lambda a: sum(a[i] > a[j] for i in range(len(a)) for j in range(i + 1, len(a)))
for label, x in zip('ABCD', (10, 12, 14, 16)):
    arr = [1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, x, 15, 13]
    s = insertion_sort_swaps(arr)
    print(label, x, 'swaps =', s, '| inversions =', inv(arr), '| exactly two:', s == 2)
print('integers x in 0..20 giving exactly 2 swaps:', [x for x in range(21) if insertion_sort_swaps([1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, x, 15, 13]) == 2])
